Thanks for confirming the issue! In retrospect, deprecating the field the way that I did was likely not the right call with the implicated change as it meant pre-existing vmfbs could successfully load + run incorrectly because the `block_shared_memory_size` was no longer used.

We can either drop the field entirely now, or keep it deprecated and continue passing it on dispatch and make sure the compiler never sets a non-zero value. That way old vmfbs will continue working as expected.

We'll always need to keep the field until we make a breaking format change. Give it a release or two of always being 0 and then we can remove support and see if anyone notices. We don't make guarantees today that artifacts from one release will work with another (though one day we will).
Oh.. wait I relanded the original change. We probably want to fix that @qedawkins to set the dynamic shared memory size to 0 always.

So anything generated + run with matching compiler and runtime versions will be consistent before and after the change. The issue is that a vmfb generated with differing versions will successfully run but produce invalid results. To enumerate the cases:

On the compiler side:
  Before:
    We set `blockSharedMemorySize` to the amount of shared memory (and use no statically allocated shared memory)
  After:
    We never populate the field (so always defaults to 0)

On the runtime side:
  Before:
    We use the `block_shared_memory_size` specified in the flatbuffer and pass that as the amount of shared memory on dispatch.
  After:
    We ignore the `block_shared_memory_size` field and always pass 0, regardless of what the deprecated flatbuffer field says. My reasoning at the time was that since we shouldn't ever be setting the deprecated field anyway, we don't want to ever accidentally double dip on memory requested.

So that means if you took an old vmfb it would still load with the new runtime changes but wouldn't get any of the shared memory it asked for, which doesn't cause faults (IDT shared memory can fault), but instead just produces garbage (unallocated) values. A newly compiled vmfb would probably work with the previous runtime though.
Ok, that makes it clear. Can we actually error out instead? I guess that would mean a version bump
I don't know what the procedure is for making a backend specific breaking format change. Do we have individual versioning per backend?
Let's not break the format - keep it deprecated for now.
(if you want to error on older files, then have the executable loader in the runtime code error out if the field is present and non-zero)

```
/* Skipping deprecated field: 'iree_hal_hip_ExportDef_block_shared_memory_size' */
```

issue.body:
### What happened?

When the flux models are compiled and executed, the generated output seems to be empty. This issue is visible from the commit https://github.com/iree-org/iree/commit/d7bb36baa9df2a4f88abc984bd8c9cc7efc3e37c


### Steps to reproduce your issue

This can be reproduced using the steps in https://github.com/nod-ai/shark-ai/blob/e3beeed98eda98aaf88eabda282f8ba6985687a8/shortfin/python/shortfin_apps/flux/README.md?plain=1#L19

### What component(s) does this issue relate to?

Compiler, Runtime

### Version information

IREE commit: 4889cb5fb73ac2e8f546ab36998a760ba2064b01

### Additional context

The issue occurs due to `sharedMemBytes` being set to 0 in the call to **hipModuleLaunchKernel**

https://github.com/iree-org/iree/commit/d7bb36baa9df2a4f88abc984bd8c9cc7efc3e37c#diff-faa5750ca692b9798a643f340a08b4bc22c7fedc5b304f4bb7d722e2df8209b8R581

issue.body:
Adds support for arch/sku specific PDL patterns to be loaded for finding and annotating ops with ranges to specialize for. This is a stopgap for a longer term solution where configuration logic uses range information directly and returns the set of ranges to specialize for itself.

Today, IREE::Codegen::BlockDynamicDims uses the divisibility info to split out static dims that kernel config uses, meaning this has to happen before this pass.

PDL modules aren't ideal for this use case because pattern rewrite sets require ownership over the module, but is lighter weight than transform dialect for this use case (basic matching + annotation). The reason for IR based patterns is two-fold

1. Arch/SKU specific ranges are often fixed to a few static best cases, meaning hand writing the ranges to annotate is fewer characters than emitting it with C++.
2. Adding support for new architectures is much faster to copy-paste an existing file and update the values than extending C++ switch statements.
